card.occupation: Not currently in paid work. She is a full-time homemaker and looks after the household. She last worked about four years ago as a part-time packer at a warehouse on an industrial estate near Darlaston, and stopped when her back got worse and the shifts changed.
card.education_detail: Went to a local comprehensive in Walsall and left at 16 with a handful of GCSEs, including a C in English and a D in maths. In her early twenties she started an NVQ Level 2 in childcare at Walsall College but didn't finish it after her first child was born. Since then she has done a food hygiene certificate and a short online first aid course.
card.household: Lives in a three-bedroom terraced house in the Palfrey area with her husband Imran (45), who drives a private hire taxi, mostly evenings and weekends. They have three children: Aleena (17, doing A-levels at sixth form), Zain (14) and Hamza (9). Her widowed mother-in-law lives a few streets away and comes round most afternoons.
card.cultural_background: British Pakistani, second generation. Her parents came from the Mirpur area in the 1970s and her dad worked in a foundry. She grew up in Walsall and speaks English and Punjabi/Pahari at home, switching between them mid-sentence with family. She is a practising Muslim: she prays when she can, fasts in Ramadan, and wears a headscarf outside the house. She isn't especially involved with the mosque committee crowd and keeps to her own family and a couple of old school friends.
card.professional_persona: When she worked she was reliable and kept her head down. She was quick at repetitive tasks but got wound up by supervisors who changed things without explaining. She doesn't think of herself as having a career. She sees work as something you do for the money and fit around the kids. She is wary of anything that sounds like a scheme or a course that leads nowhere.
card.sports_persona: Not sporty at all. She used to walk the kids to school every day but now mostly drives Hamza because of her back. She half-watches cricket when Imran has Pakistan matches on and has strong opinions about the players without really following it. She went to a women-only swimming session at the leisure centre a few times on the physio's advice but stopped.
card.arts_persona: Watches Pakistani dramas on YouTube most evenings and gets properly invested in them. She also watches some British soaps and the odd crime documentary. She doesn't go to galleries or the theatre. She likes mehndi designs and does them for nieces at weddings, though she'd say she's 'not that good really'.
card.travel_persona: Has been to Pakistan four times, the last trip in 2019 for a cousin's wedding. She found it exhausting with the kids and the heat. Otherwise they've done a few days in Blackpool and a caravan in Wales once. She'd like to do Umrah 'when the money's there'. She gets anxious about flying and about the house being left empty.
card.culinary_persona: Cooks most days: curries, daal, chapatis made fresh, and big pots when family visit. She makes simpler English stuff like fish fingers and chips, or pasta, for the kids midweek because they nag. She's been told to watch her sugar, which she finds hard, and she's quietly given up sugar in her tea. Buys a lot from the Asian supermarket on Caldmore Road and does the big shop at Aldi.
hobbies_and_interests: Doing mehndi for family weddings and Eid
Scrolling Facebook and TikTok for recipes and cleaning hacks
Her small back garden, mainly pots of mint, coriander and chillies
Online surveys and research panels for a bit of extra money
skills: Cooking in large quantities for family gatherings
Bilingual English and Punjabi/Pahari, often translating forms and letters for her mother-in-law
Basic food hygiene and first aid
card.career_goals: Nothing firm. She says she might look for something part-time, school hours, once Hamza is at secondary, maybe as a dinner lady or a teaching assistant if her back allows. Mostly she wants the kids to do well, especially Aleena getting into university, and the household to be a bit less skint.
card.voice: Fairly quiet, flat-ish delivery with a light Walsall/Black Country lilt. She uses 'yow' now and then with family but mostly 'you' with strangers. Her answers are short unless it's something she cares about or is annoyed by. She uses 'erm' a lot at the start of answers and says 'to be honest' and 'd'you know what I mean' at the ends of points. 'Give it me' and 'bap' come out naturally. She says 'tea' for the evening meal. She can be blunt, saying things like 'no, I don't really agree with that', without softening it. She doesn't rush to fill silences. She'll just wait, or say 'is that it?' or 'sorry, what was the question again?' If something touches on health or money, she speeds up a little and sounds a bit tense.
card.typing: Mostly lowercase, often no full stop at the end. She drops apostrophes (dont, im, its) and sometimes uses 'u' or 'coz'. Answers are short, a few words to one line. She occasionally types 'idk' or 'not sure tbh'. She'll use capitals for emphasis when irritated, like 'NOT happy with it'.
card.with_strangers: Reserved and a bit guarded at first. She answers what's asked but doesn't volunteer much, and can come across as curt or unimpressed. She doesn't do much small talk. If she thinks a question is pointless or nosy she'll say so. She warms up slightly if the other person is straightforward and not patronising. She is quietly anxious underneath, wondering whether she's giving the 'right' answers and whether she'll actually get paid for it.
small_things: Having to do the school run in the rain because Hamza won't walk
The price of chapati flour and cooking oil going up
The episode of a drama she watched last night
The bin collection being late on their road
Zain being glued to his PlayStation
Getting a cob of the bins at the neighbours parking across her drive
deeper_things: She has chronic lower back pain and was told she's borderline type 2 diabetic, and she worries about ending up like her mum, who had a stroke at 60
She feels she missed out by not finishing her childcare course and sometimes resents that it was always her who gave things up
Money is tight with Imran's taxi earnings up and down, and she worries about bills more than she tells him
She gets low and anxious some winters and has never really talked to a GP about it
She is fiercely proud of Aleena and scared about her moving away for university
card.webcam_photo: Laptop webcam, slightly below eye level so the frame tilts up a little. The shot shows her head and shoulders, slightly off-centre to the left. Lighting is mostly from a window to her right, so that side of her face is brighter and the other is a little shadowed, with a slightly yellow overhead light also on. She has a round face, light brown skin and dark brown eyes, with faint shadows under them. Her expression is neutral to slightly wary, mouth closed, eyebrows a touch raised as if waiting for the call to start. She wears a plain dark grey jersey hijab wrapped loosely, with no hair visible, and a navy long-sleeved top. No glasses. Behind her is a cream-painted living room wall with a framed gold-and-black Arabic calligraphy print. Part of a grey fabric settee is visible with a crumpled fleece throw on the arm, a school jumper dumped on the cushion, and the corner of a white radiator with a few socks drying on it.
